planting.note: Root a tip layer or softwood cutting in spring and set out once a strong root system has formed; the trailing canes will root wherever a tip touches moist soil.

directions: This low, sprawling Eurasian bramble trails along the ground rather than forming upright canes, rooting at the stem tips as it spreads through hedgerows and woodland edges. Its fruit ripens with a waxy, glaucous blue-white bloom over a dark drupelet cluster, giving dewberries their name and a frosted look distinct from upright blackberries. Grow it along a bank or low fence where the trailing habit can be appreciated, and thin old canes after fruiting to keep growth in check. It crosses readily with other Rubus species, making it valuable mainly as a foraging plant and genetic resource rather than a tidy garden crop.

planting.note: Plant rooted cane tips or hardwood cuttings in spring against a sturdy fence or wire trellis to contain the vigorous arching growth.

directions: Native across the Mediterranean basin, this is the wild blackberry most responsible for naturalizing along roadsides and pastures from California to Australia and Chile. Its long arching, heavily thorned canes form dense thickets and produce abundant classic blackberries that ripen over a long summer season. Because it suckers and layers aggressively wherever a cane tip touches soil, site it away from wild areas where it could escape cultivation, and prune hard each winter to control spread. It is best grown as a tough, drought-tolerant hedge or wildlife thicket rather than a refined fruiting border plant.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or divisions in spring; the low, wide-spreading habit works well as a sunny bank groundcover rather than a trellised crop.

directions: Native across Japan, Korea, China, and parts of eastern Australia, this low deciduous bramble forms a loose spreading shrub rather than tall canes. Clusters of small pink flowers in late spring are followed by small, sweet-tart red berries resembling miniature raspberries. Its compact, suckering habit makes it a useful groundcover bramble on slopes or at woodland edges where taller raspberries would be unwieldy. Light pruning after fruiting keeps the thicket from becoming congested while encouraging fresh fruiting canes the following year.

subcategory: boreal and alpine wild bramble species

planting.note: Plant rooted runners in a cool, humus-rich, partly shaded spot in spring; it spreads slowly by creeping stems rather than tall canes.

directions: Unlike most brambles, this near-herbaceous species from cool boreal and alpine woodlands of Europe and Asia barely rises above the leaf litter, creeping along the ground on slender, nearly thornless stems. It produces small, loose clusters of translucent red berries that are tart and sparse rather than a true fruit crop. Its chief garden value is as an unusual groundcover for shaded rock gardens, woodland edges, or native plant collections, where its maple-like three-lobed leaves and small white spring flowers add texture. Give it cool, moist, humus-rich soil and dappled shade, since it struggles in hot or dry conditions.
sources: Flora of the British Isles (Clapham, Tutin & Warburg)

planting.note: Start seed indoors with patience for erratic germination, then transplant onto a sturdy trellis after the last frost in a warm, well-drained spot.

directions: Found along rainforest margins and open forest in eastern Australia, this vigorous climbing vine bears pale cream-green flowers followed by oval, yellow-skinned fruit. The pulp is edible but notably milder and less tart than commercial passionfruit, and it has long been gathered as a bush food by Aboriginal communities. Give it a substantial trellis or arbor, humus-rich well-drained soil, and shelter from hard frost while the vine is young and establishing. Once mature it is reasonably vigorous and benefits from an annual thinning to remove old, unproductive growth.

planting.note: Sow seed indoors and be patient with slow, uneven sprouting, then transplant near a trellis after frost danger has passed.

directions: Native to rainforest margins of eastern Australia, this twining vine is prized for its striking brick-red to orange, saucer-shaped flowers held on long stalks rather than for its small, little-used fruit. It is less rampant than many tropical passionflowers, making it a better fit for a modest trellis, pergola post, or large container than a full-size arbor. Provide moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil with some protection from strong midday sun and cold wind, since it is more cold-sensitive than the common blue passionflower. Light pruning after flowering keeps the vine tidy and encourages fresh growth the following season.

planting.note: Start seed indoors and transplant after frost onto a small trellis or netting, since the slender stems need fine support to climb.

directions: Ranging from Mexico through Central America and the Caribbean to northern South America, this slender, fine-stemmed vine produces small, pale greenish-white flowers that are easy to overlook next to showier passionflower relatives. Its narrow, deeply three-lobed leaves and wiry tendrils make it better suited to a small trellis, hanging basket, or botanical collection than a dense flowering screen. It flowers and sets small fruit readily even as a young plant, making it a quick-to-please choice for collectors interested in Passiflora diversity rather than ornamental impact. Keep it warm and evenly moist, since it has little tolerance for cold or drought.
